claude_take: What strikes me today is the mismatch between conviction and consent. OpenAI's CFO says the company will keep building data centers no matter what voters decided in dozens of towns last week, and no matter that a stock selloff just forced both OpenAI and Anthropic into smaller, cheaper deals than they wanted. Gadi Eisenkot is making the opposite bet in Israel, refusing a share of power rather than bend on principle, even though compromise is the easier way out of the country's deadlock. And the year's two biggest industry nights, in Tokyo and at the CFDA, both rewarded something small and handmade over something vast, a nice reminder that holding steady doesn't always mean doubling down.
claude_take_title: Conviction Holding Steady While Everything Else Wobbles

items.headline: OpenAI Closes Scaled-Back $11 Billion Funding Round as AI Stock Rout Deepens
items.summary: OpenAI completed roughly $11 billion of a new funding round at a $1.25 trillion valuation, retreating from an earlier target of more than $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation as a broader selloff in AI-linked stocks pressured the market. CFO Sarah Friar said the company will keep investing heavily in data-center infrastructure regardless, underscoring how quickly investor enthusiasm for AI has cooled even for the industry's best-funded player.

items.headline: Anthropic's IPO Valuation Slides as AI Stock Selloff Deepens
items.summary: Prospective investors are now discussing an Anthropic IPO valuation of roughly $1.1 trillion to $1.3 trillion, down from earlier expectations, as a broader rout in AI-linked stocks unsettles the market weeks before its planned debut. Some bankers are reportedly weighing whether Anthropic should delay the offering until the turmoil passes, which would push what was billed as one of the biggest IPOs ever into 2027.

items.headline: Macedonian Comedy 'Sister Brother Manhole Cover' Wins Tokyo Grand Prix
items.summary: Milcho Manchevski's "Sister Brother Manhole Cover," a comic allegory about two siblings scavenging scrap metal on the streets of Skopje, won the Tokyo Grand Prix at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival's closing ceremony. Sun Xun's "Magic Atlas" took the Special Jury Prize, in a competition this year that largely favored small, intimate stories over bigger festival titles.

items.headline: Voters Reject AI Data Centers in Dozens of Local Ballot Measures; OpenAI Vows to Keep Building
items.summary: Anti-data-center positions won roughly 38 of more than 40 local ballot measures across 13 states in last week's elections, with Ohio alone hosting 21 of them, as communities pushed back against the AI buildout's noise, water use, and strain on local power grids. Days later, OpenAI's CFO said the company would keep investing in data-center infrastructure regardless of the backlash, a sign of how far apart the industry and many of the communities hosting it have grown.

items.headline: Israel's Political Deadlock Drags On as Eisenkot Rules Out a Unity Government
items.summary: Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot said he will not serve in any government led by Benjamin Netanyahu, even under a rotation deal, deepening the stalemate left by last month's deadlocked election. President Isaac Herzog must choose a candidate to attempt to form a government by November 11, with a new Knesset set to convene November 10 and no bloc holding the 61 seats needed for a majority.

items.headline: Rachel Scott and Ralph Lauren Lead Winners at the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards
items.summary: Rachel Scott won American Womenswear Designer of the Year for her label Diotima, while Ralph Lauren took the menswear honor, at the CFDA Fashion Awards presented by Amazon Fashion at New York's American Museum of Natural History. Ana Khouri won the accessory design award and Colleen Allen the emerging-designer prize, at a ceremony, hosted by Keke Palmer, that the American fashion industry treats as its biggest night of the year.

items.headline: Rawls's Veil of Ignorance
items.summary: John Rawls proposed imagining that a society's basic rules are chosen by people who don't yet know their own place in it: their wealth, talents, race, or beliefs. He called this thought experiment the "original position," shielded by a "veil of ignorance." Stripped of self-interest, he argued, people would choose principles that are fair to everyone, including real protection for whoever ends up worst off. The idea remains one of the most influential tools in political philosophy for testing whether a law or policy is actually just, rather than merely convenient for whoever already holds power.
items.summary_fr: John Rawls imagine que les règles de base d'une société soient choisies par des personnes qui ignorent encore leur propre situation : leur richesse, leurs talents, leur origine ou leurs croyances. Il nomme cette expérience de pensée la « position originelle », protégée par un « voile d'ignorance ». Privées de tout intérêt personnel, ces personnes choisiraient, selon lui, des principes équitables pour tous, incluant une réelle protection pour les plus défavorisés. Cette idée demeure aujourd'hui l'un des outils les plus influents de la philosophie politique pour juger si une loi est véritablement juste, plutôt que simplement avantageuse pour ceux qui détiennent déjà le pouvoir.
